learn.title: How Electric Vehicles Work
learn.intro: Electric vehicles are transforming transportation by reducing emissions and dependence on fossil fuels. Understanding how they operate—from electric motors to regenerative braking and charging infrastructure—is key to supporting the global shift toward clean mobility. As India accelerates EV adoption under its FAME scheme, grasping EV technology becomes essential for policymakers, students, and consumers alike.
learn.c1_title: ⚡ Electric Motors: The Heart of Motion
learn.c1_text: Unlike gasoline engines, electric motors convert electrical energy directly into motion using magnetic fields. Think of pedaling a bicycle with multiple gears—the motor adjusts torque instantly for smooth acceleration. Most EVs deliver peak torque immediately, making them faster off the line than traditional cars. A typical EV motor can reach up to 10,000 RPM, far exceeding internal combustion limits.
learn.c2_text: Regenerative braking captures kinetic energy during deceleration, converting it back into electricity instead of wasting it as heat like conventional brakes. When you ease off the accelerator, the motor acts as a generator, feeding power back into the battery. This process can recover 10–30% of energy normally lost, extending driving range significantly—especially in city traffic.
learn.c3_text: India plans to install 40,000 public EV charging stations by 2025 under the National Electric Mobility Mission Plan. Fast chargers can replenish an EV battery to 80% in under 30 minutes, while home units take 6–12 hours. The government offers subsidies up to ₹10,000 per kW for fast chargers, aiming to boost confidence among new buyers transitioning from petrol/diesel vehicles.
learn.stat1: India targets 30% EV sales by 2030 under FAME-II scheme
learn.stat2: Over 1.1 million electric cars sold globally in 2022
learn.stat3: Typical EV battery retains 80% capacity after 1,000+ charge cycles
learn.stat4: Fast DC chargers deliver up to 350 kW, adding 200+ miles in 15 mins

learn.title: Solar PV Panels Explained
learn.intro: Solar photovoltaic panels harness sunlight using the photoelectric effect to generate clean electricity without moving parts or emissions. With India poised to become a global leader in solar capacity, understanding how these panels work is crucial for students, engineers, and citizens invested in combating climate change through renewable energy adoption.
learn.c1_text: Solar cells use semiconductors—usually silicon—to absorb photons from sunlight. When a photon hits the cell, it knocks an electron loose, creating a flow of electrical current. Imagine raindrops hitting a roof gutter system—each drop triggers a cascade effect. A standard panel contains about 72 cells wired together to produce usable voltage levels for homes and grids.
learn.c2_text: Individual panels connect in series and parallel configurations to form arrays, increasing voltage and current output. Inverters convert direct current (DC) generated by panels into alternating current (AC) used by appliances and fed into the grid. Modern smart inverters also stabilize voltage fluctuations, ensuring safe and efficient integration even when clouds intermittently reduce output.
learn.c3_text: India ranks 3rd globally in rooftop solar potential with over 120 GW theoretically available. The Bhadla Solar Park in Rajasthan spans 14,000 acres and generates 2,245 MW—enough for 1.5 million homes. Under the International Solar Alliance, India aims for 280 GW solar capacity by 2030, leveraging domestic manufacturing incentives outlined in Production Linked Incentive schemes.
learn.stat1: India installed 17.4 GW solar capacity by March 2024
learn.stat2: Silicon solar cells achieve ~20% efficiency under standard test conditions
learn.stat3: Global solar capacity reached 1 TW by early 2022
learn.stat4: Bhadla Solar Park produces enough electricity for 1.5 million homes annually

learn.title: Pumped Hydro Storage Explained
learn.intro: Pumped hydro storage functions like the world's largest rechargeable battery, balancing supply and demand across power grids. It stores excess renewable energy by pumping water uphill, then releases it through turbines when needed. As India expands its renewable portfolio, mastering long-duration storage technologies becomes vital for ensuring grid reliability and maximizing clean energy utilization.
learn.c1_text: During low-demand periods, surplus electricity powers pumps that move water from a lower reservoir to an upper one, storing potential energy—like winding up a giant spring. When demand peaks, releasing the water drives hydroelectric turbines to generate power quickly. This cycle repeats daily, offering rapid response capabilities unmatched by other large-scale storage methods.
learn.c2_text: Modern pumped storage plants operate at 70–85% round-trip efficiency, losing some energy due to friction and pump/turbine losses. Crucially, they can ramp up full output within minutes—faster than any thermal plant. These facilities often provide ancillary services like frequency regulation, helping stabilize grids as variable renewables increase their share of total generation capacity.
learn.c3_title: 🇮🇳 Green Energy Corridors and Storage Plans
learn.c3_text: India has identified 96 potential sites for pumped hydro projects totaling 96 GW capacity, primarily in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. The government includes storage targets in its renewable energy plans, with the Green Energy Corridor project enhancing transmission infrastructure. As part of its net-zero pledge by 2070, India seeks hybrid renewable-plus-storage models to ensure 24x7 clean power availability nationwide.
learn.stat1: World's largest pumped storage is China's 22.5 GW Three Gorges complex
learn.stat2: Pumped hydro provides over 90% of global grid-scale energy storage today
learn.stat3: India identified 96 GW theoretical pumped hydro potential across 96 sites

learn.title: Sodium-Ion Batteries Explained
learn.intro: Sodium-ion batteries offer a promising low-cost alternative to lithium-ion technology, leveraging abundant sodium resources instead of scarce materials. As India scales EV manufacturing and grid storage ambitions, exploring sustainable chemistries like sodium-ion could diversify supply chains and reduce reliance on critical minerals while maintaining performance standards for future applications.
learn.c1_text: Sodium is found in seawater and common salt deposits worldwide, making it far more accessible than lithium. Sodium-ion cells function similarly to lithium counterparts but use Prussian Blue analogues or layered oxides as electrode materials. Their raw material costs are roughly one-third those of lithium iron phosphate batteries, offering significant economic advantages for mass deployment in stationary storage systems.
learn.c2_text: While sodium-ion batteries currently deliver slightly lower energy density (~120 Wh/kg vs ~160 Wh/kg for LFP), they perform better at sub-zero temperatures and show improved safety profiles. They’re ideal for short-distance EVs, home energy storage, and backup systems where weight isn’t critical. Recent breakthroughs have extended cycle life beyond 4,000 charges with minimal degradation.
learn.c3_text: Under India’s National Mission on Strategic Materials, researchers are developing indigenous sodium-ion pilot projects to complement lithium-cell initiatives under the PLI scheme. With limited lithium reserves, India imports over 90% of its lithium needs. Government-backed R&D focuses on adapting sodium technology for two-wheelers and three-wheelers, which dominate Indian roads and represent massive near-term market opportunities.
learn.stat1: Sodium makes up 2.6% of Earth's crust compared to 0.006% for lithium
learn.stat2: Sodium-ion batteries achieve ~120 Wh/kg energy density today
learn.stat3: India imports 90%+ of lithium required for EV battery production
learn.stat4: Cycle life exceeds 4,000 charges with less than 20% capacity loss

learn.title: Hydrogen Fuel Cells Explained
learn.intro: Hydrogen fuel cells generate clean electricity through electrochemical reactions, producing only water vapor as waste. They’re especially valuable for heavy transport sectors hard to electrify. With India launching a National Green Hydrogen Mission, understanding fuel cell principles becomes increasingly important for engineers, policymakers, and innovators shaping the nation’s clean energy future.
learn.c1_text: Fuel cells combine hydrogen and oxygen at separate electrodes separated by a proton-exchange membrane. At the anode, hydrogen splits into protons and electrons; electrons travel through an external circuit generating current, while protons pass through the membrane. At the cathode, they recombine with oxygen to form water—a process first demonstrated by Sir William Grove in 1839 and now powering everything from buses to backup generators.
learn.c2_text: In hydrogen-powered vehicles, fuel stacks deliver continuous power without combustion noise or vibration. Unlike batteries, refueling takes just 3–5 minutes regardless of tank size, offering ranges comparable to diesel trucks. Companies like Toyota and Hyundai use multi-stack designs delivering 80–150 kW output. These systems operate efficiently across wide temperature ranges, making them suitable for extreme climates and industrial environments.
learn.c3_text: Launched in 2023, India’s $2.3 billion National Green Hydrogen Mission targets 5 MMT annual production by 2030. Plans include setting up mega hubs near renewable-rich regions like Gujarat and Rajasthan. Heavy-duty transport corridors may see early adoption, with Indian Oil Corporation testing hydrogen trucks along Delhi-Mumbai routes. The mission also supports green ammonia exports, positioning India as a future clean fuel hub for Asia.
learn.stat1: Hydrogen fuel cells emit only water vapor during operation
learn.stat2: Refueling hydrogen vehicles takes 3–5 minutes versus 30+ mins for EV fast-charging
learn.stat3: India allocated $2.3 billion for National Green Hydrogen Mission
learn.stat4: Green hydrogen production cost fell below $3/kg in some regions by 2023

learn.title: Power Purchase Agreements Explained
learn.intro: Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) are long-term contracts that enable corporations and utilities to buy renewable energy directly from generators. They de-risk investments and lock in stable pricing. In India, where corporate PPAs are gaining traction amid ambitious renewable targets, understanding PPA structures helps businesses navigate energy transitions while supporting grid-scale clean power expansion.
learn.c1_text: A PPA defines terms including price, volume, delivery point, and duration—typically 15–25 years. Buyers receive clean energy attributes and often hedge against volatile fossil fuel prices. For sellers, PPAs guarantee revenue streams, enabling project financing without upfront capital. Think of it like leasing farmland—you pay for predictable yields rather than owning assets, reducing financial risk for both parties involved.
learn.c2_text: Virtual PPAs settle financially based on market prices without physical delivery, allowing companies to claim environmental benefits remotely. Physical PPAs involve actual electricity transfer via grid connections. Sleeved PPAs add intermediaries handling logistics. Corporations like Google and Microsoft signed over $23 billion in clean energy PPAs globally last year, driving demand for standardized contract templates and transparent reporting frameworks.
learn.c3_text: India launched its first corporate renewable energy PPA framework in 2022, allowing open access consumers to buy green power directly. Over 50 commercial establishments have registered since inception. Major adopters include IT parks and manufacturing units seeking ESG compliance. The CEA issued guidelines simplifying wheeling charges, encouraging cross-state transactions. State discoms are also signing bulk PPAs to meet RPO obligations efficiently.
learn.stat1: Corporate PPAs accounted for over 35% of new U.S. renewable capacity additions in 2022
learn.stat2: India’s first corporate RE PPA was signed in 2022 after regulatory clarity emerged
